content: The hypogastrium, also referred to as the hypogastric region, pubic region, or suprapubic region, is a specific area of the human abdomen located below the navel. Its lower boundary is defined by the pubic bone. Causes of Hypogastric Pain: Bladder stones Bladder cancer, specifically transitional cell carcinoma Cystitis Diarrhea Diverticulum Dysentery Endometriosis Uterine fibroids Menstruation Ovarian cancer Ovarian cysts Ovarian torsion Pelvic inflammatory disease Management of Hypogastric Pain: Begin the evaluation of acute abdominal pain with a rapid assessment of the patient’s airway, breathing, and circulation (ABC) to identify unstable patients. In patients over 50 years of age, consider abdominal aortic aneurysm, mesenteric ischemia, and malignancy as potential causes, as these are less common in younger individuals. Perform pelvic and testicular examinations in patients presenting with lower abdominal pain. Reassess high-risk patients who were initially diagnosed with pain of unclear etiology. A thorough history, precise characterization of the pain, and a detailed physical examination are essential for narrowing the differential diagnosis. In HIV-positive patients, correlate the CD4 count with the most likely underlying pathology. For females of childbearing age, order a pregnancy test before proceeding with a CT scan. In pregnant patients, use ultrasound or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) to avoid radiation exposure. If prior tests are inconclusive and appendicitis is suspected, proceed with either laparoscopy or a limited CT scan. Consider peritonitis in patients with cervical motion tenderness, as this finding is not specific to pelvic inflammatory disease. Suspect an abdominal aortic aneurysm in older patients with abdominal pain and a history of tobacco use. Suspect acute mesenteric ischemia or acute pancreatitis in patients with poorly localized pain that is disproportionate to physical findings. Recommend initial imaging studies based on the location of the abdominal pain: Use ultrasonography for patients with right upper quadrant pain. Use CT with intravenous contrast for adults with acute right lower quadrant pain. Use CT with oral and intravenous contrast for patients with left lower quadrant pain. Order an ECG for older patients with upper abdominal pain and high cardiac risk factors. Administer narcotic analgesia for patients presenting to the emergency department with moderate to severe abdominal pain. Perform diagnostic paracentesis (including cell count, differential count, Gram stain, culture, bilirubin, and albumin analysis) in patients with ascites and abdominal pain to rule out spontaneous bacterial peritonitis. Actions to Avoid: Do not fail to evaluate elderly patients even in the presence of overt clinical signs. Avoid over-reliance on laboratory tests, as they are only adjunctive tools. Do not delay initial interventions. Do not routinely order blood cultures for all patients. Do not delay resuscitation or surgical consultation for critically ill patients while waiting for imaging results. Do not restrict the differential diagnosis of abdominal pain based solely on its location; for example, right-sided structures may refer pain to the left abdomen.
